/journal/beanmarkd-is-open-to-everyone.body:
Beanmarkd started with a simple frustration: you spend real money on a beautiful bag, brew something you love, and a month later you can't remember which one it was.

We're **soft-launching on 26 June 2026** — opening the doors to a small group first while we polish the experience. If you'd like to try it, email the Beanmarkd team and we'll get you in.

## What you can do today

- **Log a brew** in seconds — one rating, everything else optional.
- **Tap in** to a roaster's roast drop to capture the *verified* roast date automatically.
- **Toast** the brews your friends are loving and follow people whose taste you trust.
- **Track freshness** — every brew shows how many days off roast the beans were.

## Where we're headed

We're building toward a world where every great coffee has a traceable story, from roast drop to last cup. Expect deeper roaster collaborations, smarter discovery, and more ways to remember what you loved.

> No snobbery. No checkout. Just better ways to remember great coffee while the clock is still warm.

Interested in an early invite? Email the Beanmarkd team.
/journal/beanmarkd-is-open-to-everyone.excerpt: Beanmarkd is soft-launching on 26 June 2026 — the shared memory for the beans you brew. Here's what you can do on day one, and how to get in.
/journal/beanmarkd-is-open-to-everyone.title: Beanmarkd is in soft-launch

/journal/dialling-in-aeropress.body:
The AeroPress is the brewer that travels well and never sulks. It's quick, easy to clean, and remarkably hard to mess up, which makes it the perfect place to practise the four dials without pressure. It brews a smooth, low-acidity cup somewhere between filter and espresso in body.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 15 g
- **Water:** 220 g
- **Temperature:** **85 °C** — deliberately cooler, for a sweeter, rounder cup
- **Total time:** about **2:00**
- **Grind:** **medium-fine** — a touch finer than table salt

Add coffee, pour the water, give it a gentle stir or swirl, let it steep, then press slowly and stop when you hear a hiss.

## Dial it in

The AeroPress gives you lots of dials, so change just one at a time. **Time, grind and temperature** are the easy ones here:

- **Tastes sour or weak?** Under-extracted. Steep a little **longer**, grind **finer**, or bump the water **hotter** (towards 90–95 °C, especially for light roasts).
- **Tastes bitter or harsh?** Over-extracted. **Shorten** the steep, grind **coarser**, or pull the temperature **down**.

Worth knowing: James Hoffmann's own AeroPress recipe is even simpler — a small dose (around 11 g to 200 g), a couple of minutes' steep, a gentle swirl rather than a vigorous stir, then a slow press. The lesson from it is that gentleness and a clean technique beat fuss. Press slowly; forcing it fast muddies the cup.

Many people also love the inverted method (assembling upside down so nothing drips early). It's optional — the standard way works fine to start.

## Common mistakes

- Pressing hard and fast. A slow, calm press of 20–30 seconds tastes far better.
- Using water straight off the boil on a dark roast and scorching it bitter.
- Stirring aggressively and dislodging the filter or bruising the grounds.
- Grinding too fine, which makes the press a workout and over-extracts.
- Forgetting to rinse the paper filter — a quick rinse removes papery taste.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in pour-over](/journal/dialling-in-pour-over) · Next: [Dialling in the French press](/journal/dialling-in-french-press) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — "The Ultimate AeroPress Technique" (gentle press, swirl, short steep)
- *The World Atlas of Coffee* (immersion brewing, temperature by roast level)
/journal/dialling-in-aeropress.excerpt: Forgiving, fast and almost impossible to ruin — the AeroPress is the friendliest brewer there is. Start at 15 g to 220 g with cooler water and a gentle press.
/journal/dialling-in-aeropress.title: Dialling in the AeroPress

/journal/dialling-in-batch-drip.body:
The drip machine is the workhorse of the kitchen and the office: switch it on, walk away, come back to a pot of coffee. It's an immersion-meets-percolation hybrid, and a good one makes genuinely excellent filter coffee for more than one person. Most disappointing pots aren't the machine's fault — they're under-dosed.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 30 g
- **Water:** 500 g (about a **1:16.7** ratio — the SCA "golden ratio")
- **Temperature:** **94 °C** (most machines sit in the SCA's 92–96 °C window)
- **Brew time:** around **5:00**
- **Grind:** **medium** — like table salt, the same ballpark as pour-over

Weigh the coffee, use filtered water, and let the machine run its cycle.

## Dial it in

Batch brew gives you fewer dials in the moment because the machine fixes the temperature and flow. So **ratio and grind** do most of the work:

- **Tastes weak, sour or flat?** Under-extracted (and usually under-dosed). Use **more coffee** first — bump towards 1:15 — then grind **finer** if it's still thin.
- **Tastes bitter or harsh?** Over-extracted. Grind **coarser**, or pull the ratio back towards 1:18.

Two machine-specific tips. **Fill the basket evenly** so water doesn't bore a channel through a lopsided bed. And **match the batch to the basket** — brewing a single mug in a machine built for a full carafe gives a shallow bed that the water rushes through, tasting weak and sour. If you only want one cup, a pour-over is often better.

## Common mistakes

- Under-dosing — the number one cause of weak, sad office coffee. Weigh it.
- A flat or tilted bed of grounds, which channels.
- Leaving the carafe on the hotplate, which stews the coffee bitter. Decant to a flask.
- Never descaling. Scale ruins both temperature and flow over time.
- Old water-line guesswork instead of weighing — markings lie, scales don't.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in cold brew](/journal/dialling-in-cold-brew) · Next: [Dialling in tea](/journal/dialling-in-tea) →*

## Sources

- Specialty Coffee Association — Golden Cup standard (ratio, 92–96 °C, contact time)
- James Hoffmann — *The World Atlas of Coffee* (batch / filter brewing)
/journal/dialling-in-batch-drip.excerpt: The trusty filter machine makes great coffee for a crowd if you treat it kindly. Start at 30 g to 500 g — the SCA golden ratio — at 94 °C, and the main thing to fix is a stingy dose.
/journal/dialling-in-batch-drip.title: Dialling in batch and drip

/journal/dialling-in-chai.body:
Masala chai isn't a tea bag dropped in hot milk — it's a small pot of tea, spices, water and milk simmered together until everything melds. It's warming, fragrant and endlessly personal: every household has its own spice balance. That's the joy of dialling it in. There's no snobbery here, just your kitchen and your taste.

## Your starting point

- **Tea:** 4 g of strong black tea (Assam or a robust breakfast blend works well)
- **Water:** 150 ml
- **Milk:** 150 ml (a roughly 1:1 water-to-milk pot)
- **Spices:** whole — a few crushed green cardamom pods, a small piece of cinnamon, a clove or two, a slice of fresh ginger
- **Simmer:** about **4:00**

Lightly crush the whole spices and simmer them with the water first to wake them up, add the tea, then pour in the milk and bring it back to a gentle simmer. Strain into your cup.

## Dial it in

Chai has more dials than coffee — tea strength, spice level, milk ratio and simmer time — so move one at a time:

- **Tastes weak or watery?** Under-brewed. **Simmer longer**, use **more tea**, or lean the ratio towards **more water** before the milk so the tea brews properly.
- **Tastes harsh or over-stewed?** Over-brewed. **Shorten** the simmer and ease off the tea.
- **Spice too faint?** Crush the whole spices more and **simmer them longer in the water** before the tea and milk go in — that's where the aroma comes from.
- **Want it creamier?** Shift the ratio towards **more milk**; for a stronger, brighter brew, more water.

Add any sugar near the end and taste as you go — chai is meant to be adjusted in the pot.

## Common mistakes

- Using ground spice powder when you want a fresh, aromatic cup — whole spices, lightly crushed, are far better.
- Adding milk too early so the tea never properly brews. Brew in water first, then add milk.
- Boiling hard for ages, which turns the tea bitter and stewed. A gentle simmer is plenty.
- Skimping on the tea so the spices drown it — chai should still taste of tea.
- Forgetting to strain, and getting a mouthful of cardamom husk.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in matcha](/journal/dialling-in-matcha) · Next: [Dialling in hot chocolate](/journal/dialling-in-hot-chocolate) →*

## Sources

- Swasthi's Recipes — masala chai with whole spices (ratio, simmer method)
- Tea for Turmeric / Masala and Chai — water-to-milk ratio and spice technique
/journal/dialling-in-chai.excerpt: Proper masala chai is simmered, not steeped — tea and whole spices brewed together in water and milk. Start at 4 g tea, 150 ml water and 150 ml milk, simmer four minutes, and build the spice to taste.
/journal/dialling-in-chai.title: Dialling in chai

/journal/dialling-in-cold-brew.body:
Cold brew is coffee made the lazy way, and that's a compliment. There's no kettle, no timer to watch, no skill on the night — you just combine coffee and cold water and wait. Time replaces heat, so it extracts slowly and gently, giving a smooth, sweet, low-acidity drink that keeps for days in the fridge.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 100 g
- **Water:** 1000 g / 1 litre (a **1:10** ratio — this is a strong concentrate)
- **Steep:** **16 hours**, in the fridge
- **Grind:** **very coarse** — chunky, like coarse sea salt

Stir the grounds and cold water together so everything's wet, cover, and leave it in the fridge. After 16 hours, strain through a paper filter or muslin and discard the grounds.

At 1:10 you've made a concentrate. Dilute it to taste when you serve — start around 1:1 with water, milk or ice and adjust.

## Dial it in

Your dials here are **steep time and ratio** (grind matters too, but coarse is your safety net). Heat isn't in play.

- **Tastes weak, sour or watery?** Under-extracted. Steep **longer** (towards 18–20 hours), or use **more coffee** (a tighter ratio like 1:8). Check you didn't over-dilute when serving.
- **Tastes bitter, woody or overpowering?** Over-extracted. Steep **less** (towards 12–14 hours), grind **coarser**, or dilute more when serving.

Because it's so slow and forgiving, big swings are safe — change the steep by a few hours, not minutes.

## Common mistakes

- Grinding too fine, which over-extracts even cold and makes straining a nightmare of sludge.
- Steeping at room temperature for a long time — fridge-steep for clean flavour and safety.
- Forgetting it's a concentrate and drinking it neat, then declaring it too strong.
- Steeping far too long (over a day) and ending up bitter and woody.
- A lazy strain. Paper or cloth gives a clean cup; a coarse sieve leaves grit.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in the moka pot](/journal/dialling-in-moka-pot) · Next: [Dialling in batch / drip](/journal/dialling-in-batch-drip) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — *The World Atlas of Coffee* (cold brew, immersion and ratio)
- Counter Culture Coffee — cold brew guide (ratio, coarse grind, steep time)
/journal/dialling-in-cold-brew.excerpt: Smooth, sweet and low in acidity, cold brew is the most hands-off method going. Start at 100 g to 1000 g, steep 16 hours in the fridge, and let time do all the work.
/journal/dialling-in-cold-brew.title: Dialling in cold brew

/journal/dialling-in-espresso.body:
Espresso is coffee under pressure: a small dose, a lot of force, a short, intense shot. It's the most sensitive brew in this series because tiny changes show up loudly in the cup. That's also what makes it satisfying to dial in — and a good scale plus a grinder you can adjust are all you really need.

## Your starting point

- **Dose:** 18 g of coffee in the basket
- **Yield:** 36 g of espresso out (a **1:2** ratio)
- **Shot time:** about **28 seconds** from the moment the pump starts
- **Temperature:** **93 °C**
- **Grind:** **fine** — fine enough to resist the water

Weigh both the dose going in and the shot coming out. Timing alone won't tell you what happened; the scale will.

## Dial it in

With espresso, **grind is your main dial** and the shot time is your feedback. Lock the dose at 18 g and the yield at 36 g, then chase the timing with the grinder:

- **Shot runs fast (under ~25 s) and tastes sour or thin?** Under-extracted. Grind **finer** to slow the water down and pull more out.
- **Shot runs slow (over ~32 s) and tastes bitter or harsh?** Over-extracted. Grind **coarser** to speed it up.

Get the time into the 25–32 second window first, then taste. If it's still a touch sour, you can nudge the yield up (try 18 g → 40 g) or the temperature up a degree. Still bitter, pull a shorter shot (18 g → 32 g) or drop the temperature. Move one dial at a time.

## Common mistakes

- Stopping the shot by time instead of weight — you can't diagnose what you don't measure.
- Changing dose, grind and time all at once.
- A sloppy puck: uneven dose or no level tamp causes channelling, where water bores a hole and the shot tastes both sour and bitter at once.
- Expecting one grind setting to work forever — beans drift as they age, so re-dial every new bag.
- Judging a shot by crema alone. Crema looks nice but taste is the verdict.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew — then jot the grind setting that worked for this bag.

*Previous: [Dialling in: the four dials](/journal/dialling-in-the-four-dials) · Next: [Dialling in pour-over](/journal/dialling-in-pour-over) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — *The World Atlas of Coffee* (espresso ratios and extraction)
- Specialty Coffee Association — espresso dose/yield/time guidance
- Barista Hustle — espresso dialling-in and channelling
/journal/dialling-in-espresso.excerpt: Espresso is the fussiest drink to dial in and the most rewarding. Start at 18 g in, 36 g out, about 28 seconds, and let the grinder do the work from there.
/journal/dialling-in-espresso.title: Dialling in espresso

/journal/dialling-in-french-press.body:
The French press is the most honest brewer in the kitchen: coffee, hot water, time, plunge. Because the grounds steep in all the water at once, you get a heavy, rich, full-bodied cup. Its only reputation problem is sludge at the bottom — and there's a tidy fix for that.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 30 g
- **Water:** 500 g (about a **1:16** ratio)
- **Temperature:** **95 °C**
- **Steep:** **4:00**
- **Grind:** **coarse** — like breadcrumbs or rough sea salt

Pour all the water over the coffee, start the timer, and leave it alone for four minutes.

## Dial it in

With full immersion, **grind and steep time** are your main dials, and temperature is the fine-tune:

- **Tastes sour, thin or weak?** Under-extracted. Grind a little **finer**, **extend** the steep past 4:00, or use **hotter** water.
- **Tastes bitter, muddy or astringent?** Over-extracted. Grind **coarser**, **shorten** the steep, or ease the temperature down.

To lose the sludge, borrow James Hoffmann's clean-cup technique. At four minutes, gently **break the crust** with a spoon (two slow stirs) and the grounds will start to sink. Then **skim** the foam and floating bits off the top — that layer holds the finest, most bitter particles. Now leave it to settle for another five minutes or so. Finally, rest the plunger just on the surface (don't push down hard) and **decant** slowly, leaving the last sediment-heavy splash behind. The result is a clean cup with all the body and none of the grit.

## Common mistakes

- Plunging hard to the bottom, which forces fine particles up and muddies the cup.
- Grinding too fine, so the mesh can't hold it back and you get silt.
- Leaving the coffee sitting on the grounds in the press after pouring — it keeps extracting and turns bitter. Decant it all into a separate vessel.
- Skipping the skim. It's the single step that transforms the cup.
- Cold water or a cold pot dragging the temperature down and souring the brew.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in the AeroPress](/journal/dialling-in-aeropress) · Next: [Dialling in the moka pot](/journal/dialling-in-moka-pot) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — "The Ultimate French Press Technique" (break the crust, skim, decant)
- *The World Atlas of Coffee* (immersion brewing, coarse grind)
/journal/dialling-in-french-press.excerpt: Full-bodied, rich and dead simple — the French press is pure immersion. Start at 30 g to 500 g, steep four minutes, and use one clever skim to lose the sludge.
/journal/dialling-in-french-press.title: Dialling in the French press

/journal/dialling-in-hot-chocolate.body:
Hot chocolate is the gentle end of this series — no extraction to balance, no bitterness to fear, just chocolate and warm milk. The whole game is richness and smoothness, and the difference between a watery letdown and a proper hug in a mug comes down to a few easy choices.

## Your starting point

- **Chocolate:** 3 spoons (about **3 teaspoons**) of cocoa powder, chocolate flakes or chopped chocolate
- **Milk:** 250 ml
- **Temperature:** warm to about **65 °C** — steaming, with tiny bubbles at the edge, never a rolling boil

If you're using cocoa powder, first mix it with a splash of the milk (or a little hot water) into a smooth paste, then whisk that into the rest of the warm milk. Paste first is the whole secret to no lumps.

## Dial it in

Your dials are simply **how much chocolate, what kind, and the milk**:

- **Tastes thin or weak?** Add **more chocolate**, or use a richer milk (whole or a barista oat) for body.
- **Too rich or claggy?** Ease back the chocolate, or loosen it with a little more milk.
- **Not sweet enough?** Cocoa powder is unsweetened, so add a little sugar; flakes and chopped bars often bring their own sweetness, so taste before adding.
- **Lumpy?** You added powder straight to hot milk. Always make the **paste first**.

Powder vs flakes vs melted: **powder** is quick and gives a clean cocoa hit; **flakes** melt smoothly and are usually pre-sweetened; **melted real chocolate** is the most luxurious and silky, but needs gentle heat and steady whisking so it doesn't seize. Keep the milk below the boil whichever you use — scalded milk tastes flat and forms a skin.

## Common mistakes

- Tipping cocoa powder straight into hot milk and fighting lumps forever. Paste first.
- Boiling the milk, which scorches it and dulls the flavour. Aim for steaming, ~65 °C.
- Forgetting cocoa powder is unsweetened and serving it bitter and sad.
- Using skimmed milk and wondering why it's thin — fat carries the richness.
- Walking away from melting chocolate; it can catch and seize. Low heat, keep whisking.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in chai](/journal/dialling-in-chai)*

## Sources

- Celebrating Sweets / Laura Fuentes — homemade hot chocolate (cocoa vs chocolate, paste method)
- U.S. Dairy — hot chocolate with cocoa powder (milk heating, ~steaming not boiling)
/journal/dialling-in-hot-chocolate.excerpt: The cosiest drink to dial in, and the easiest. Start at 3 spoons of cocoa to 250 ml of milk warmed to about 65 °C — then it's just powder, flakes or melted, and how rich you like it.
/journal/dialling-in-hot-chocolate.title: Dialling in hot chocolate

/journal/dialling-in-matcha.body:
Matcha is different from every other drink in this series: you don't steep it and strain it away, you whisk the powdered leaf straight into water and drink the lot. That's why it's vivid green and full-bodied — and why the smoothness depends less on a ratio and more on your whisking. The good news is the technique takes minutes to learn.

## Your starting point (usucha — thin matcha)

- **Matcha:** 2 g (about **1 chashaku scoop**, or roughly half a teaspoon)
- **Water:** 70 ml
- **Temperature:** **80 °C** (never boiling — it scalds matcha bitter)
- **Whisk:** about **20 seconds**, until frothy
- **For a matcha latte:** make the usucha as above, then add ~150 ml of warmed or steamed milk

Sift the powder first to break up lumps, add the water, and whisk briskly in a quick **"W" or "M" motion** from the wrist — not a round stir — until a fine, even foam forms on top. Drink it soon, while the froth is alive.

## Dial it in

There's no extraction to chase here, so your dials are **ratio, temperature and whisking**:

- **Tastes thin, watery or flat?** Use a little **more powder** (or slightly less water) for a fuller, more vivid cup.
- **Tastes harsh, bitter or chalky?** The usual culprits are **water too hot** (drop towards 75–80 °C) or **under-whisking** that leaves gritty undissolved powder. Cool the water and whisk more thoroughly.
- **Gritty or lumpy?** Always **sift** the powder before whisking, and don't skimp on the 20 seconds.

For a latte, the milk softens and sweetens everything, so you can run the base a touch stronger so the matcha still comes through.

## Common mistakes

- Boiling water. The fastest way to a bitter, astringent bowl. Cool it to ~80 °C.
- Not sifting — lumps that never whisk out leave a chalky finish.
- Stirring in circles instead of the brisk back-and-forth whisk that builds froth.
- Letting it sit; matcha separates and the powder sinks. Whisk, then drink.
- Using cooking-grade matcha for a straight bowl — ceremonial grade is far smoother to drink neat.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in tea](/journal/dialling-in-tea) · Next: [Dialling in chai](/journal/dialling-in-chai) →*

## Sources

- Ippodo Tea — how to make usucha (thin matcha) ratio and method
- Naoki Matcha / Tezumi — usucha preparation, water temperature, whisking technique
/journal/dialling-in-matcha.excerpt: Matcha is whisked, not steeped — you drink the whole leaf. Start at 2 g (one scoop) to 70 ml of 80 °C water, whisk for twenty seconds, and the smoothness lives in the technique.
/journal/dialling-in-matcha.title: Dialling in matcha

/journal/dialling-in-moka-pot.body:
The moka pot is a kitchen icon: that octagonal aluminium pot that gurgles on the hob and fills the room with coffee. It makes a strong, concentrated, almost syrupy brew — not quite espresso, but rich and bold. Its bad reputation for bitterness is almost always about heat, and that's easy to fix.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 17 g (fill the basket level, don't tamp)
- **Water:** 150 ml — and **pre-heat it** before it goes in the base
- **Heat:** **medium**, leaning low
- **Time:** around **5:00** start to finish
- **Grind:** **fine-medium** — finer than filter, coarser than espresso

Start with hot water in the base, the basket filled and levelled, lid open, on a gentle flame.

## Dial it in

The big lever on a moka pot is **heat**, with grind close behind. Borrow James Hoffmann's two key moves: **start with pre-heated water** so the coffee isn't slowly cooked while the base warms up, and keep the **heat low**. Then taste:

- **Tastes sour or thin?** Under-extracted. Grind a touch **finer**, or let it run a little **warmer** so extraction completes.
- **Tastes bitter or burnt?** Over-extracted (or scorched). Grind **coarser**, drop the **heat**, and pre-heat the water if you weren't.

Watch the top chamber: when the coffee starts streaming and turns from dark to a paler, honeyed colour, it's nearly done. Take it off the heat and cool the base (a damp cloth or a splash of cold water on the bottom) to stop the brew cleanly before it sputters and burns.

## Common mistakes

- Cold water and high heat — the classic bitterness combo. Pre-heat and go low.
- Tamping the grounds. The basket is dosed by volume; just fill and level it.
- Walking away. The end comes fast; stay and pull it off in time.
- Letting it sputter and steam at the end, which scorches the last of the brew.
- Screwing the pot together over a hot base with bare hands — use the handle and a cloth.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in the French press](/journal/dialling-in-french-press) · Next: [Dialling in cold brew](/journal/dialling-in-cold-brew) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — "The Ultimate Moka Pot Technique" (pre-heated water, low heat)
- *The World Atlas of Coffee* (stovetop / moka brewing)

/journal/dialling-in-pour-over.body:
Pour-over is the clearest window into a coffee. With a V60 and a paper filter you get a clean, layered cup that shows off the bright, fruity notes other methods hide. It looks ceremonial, but it's really just water, time and a steady hand.

## Your starting point

- **Coffee:** 20 g
- **Water:** 320 g (a **1:16** ratio)
- **Temperature:** **94 °C**
- **Bloom:** pour about 40 g of water and wait **40 seconds**
- **Total brew time:** around **2:45**
- **Grind:** **medium** — like table salt

After the bloom, pour the rest in smooth stages, finishing your pours by about 1:45 and letting it draw down to roughly 2:45.

## Dial it in

For pour-over, **grind and total time** are your most useful dials, and the drawdown time tells you a lot:

- **Drains fast (well under 2:30), tastes sour or watery?** Under-extracted. Grind **finer** so the water lingers, or pour a little more slowly.
- **Drains slow (well past 3:15), tastes bitter or hollow?** Over-extracted. Grind **coarser**, or pour faster so the bed isn't choked.

Two approaches worth borrowing. **James Hoffmann's V60** uses a generous bloom and a gentle swirl to settle the bed evenly, then a steady continuous pour — simple and repeatable. **Tetsu Kasuya's 4:6 method** splits the water into 40% (the first two pours, which set sweetness vs acidity) and 60% (the last pours, which set strength): smaller first pour for sweetness, larger for acidity; fewer late pours for a lighter cup. Try both and keep the one your beans prefer.

## Common mistakes

- Pouring too fast and gouging the coffee bed, which causes channelling and a thin cup.
- Skipping the bloom — fresh coffee releases CO2 that pushes water away until it's degassed.
- Letting the grounds climb high up the paper and stranding them dry; a swirl keeps the bed flat.
- Water off the boil sitting too long, brewing cold and sour.
- Eyeballing the water. A scale on the drip tray makes this trivially repeatable.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in espresso](/journal/dialling-in-espresso) · Next: [Dialling in AeroPress](/journal/dialling-in-aeropress) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — "Ultimate V60 Technique" (bloom, swirl, continuous pour); *The World Atlas of Coffee*
- Tetsu Kasuya — the 4:6 method (2016 World Brewers Cup)
- Specialty Coffee Association — brewing ratio and contact time

/journal/dialling-in-tea.body:
Tea is the gentlest thing to dial in, with one catch: different teas want different water temperatures, and ignoring that is what turns a lovely cup bitter. Get the heat right for the type and almost everything else falls into place. Loose leaf or a bag — both are completely fine.

## Your starting point

- **Tea:** 3 g of loose leaf, or 1 tea bag
- **Water:** 250 ml
- **Steep:** about **3:00**
- **Temperature — match it to the type:**
  - Green tea: **~80 °C** (boiling water scorches it)
  - Black tea: **~95 °C**
  - Oolong: **~90 °C**
  - Herbal / fruit infusions: **~100 °C** (full boil — they need it)

To cool just-boiled water for green tea, let it stand a couple of minutes, or splash in a little cold.

## Dial it in

For tea, **time and temperature** are your dials; the leaf-to-water ratio is fairly steady. The same sour/bitter logic applies, with one extra word — astringency, that dry, mouth-puckering edge:

- **Tastes weak, thin or sour?** Under-extracted. Steep a little **longer**, use slightly **more** leaf, or — within the type's range — **hotter** water.
- **Tastes bitter or astringent (drying)?** Over-extracted, almost always too hot or too long. **Shorten** the steep and bring the **temperature down** for that type.

A bonus with good loose leaf: you can re-steep it two or three times, and the flavour shifts each time. Treat each steep as its own little dial-in.

## Common mistakes

- Boiling water on green tea — the single most common way to ruin it. Cool it to ~80 °C.
- Leaving the bag or leaves in the cup the whole time, so it keeps stewing past bitter. Take them out.
- Not enough room for loose leaf to unfurl — give it space, not a tight ball.
- Reheated or long-boiled water, which tastes flat. Fresh water steeps brighter.
- One steep time for every tea. Delicate greens want less; herbals want more.

Save this as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Previous: [Dialling in batch / drip](/journal/dialling-in-batch-drip) · Next: [Dialling in matcha](/journal/dialling-in-matcha) →*

## Sources

- Art of Tea — recommended steep times and temperatures by type
- ArtfulTea — tea brewing temperature guide (green/black/oolong/herbal)

/journal/in-the-cup-with-little-fern.body:
Our community-spotlight series highlights the roasters that Beanmarkd drinkers keep brewing — and the people behind the beans.

## Why this one

Little Fern shows up again and again on shelves, with brews that score high across very different methods. That kind of consistency is hard, and it usually means someone is paying close attention to sourcing and roast.

## On process

> "We pick for clarity. If the origin did something special, our job is to stay out of the way."

It's a philosophy you can taste — and one that lines up neatly with how Beanmarkd thinks about provenance.

## Brew it yourself

Browse their beans, see what the community rated highest, and log your own brew. Spotlights are editorial only — there's no checkout here, just coffee worth remembering.
